nameStory: The file yoldia gets its name from its shell's surface, which feels rough like a metal file when you run your finger along it. The genus name 'Yoldia' honors Danish naturalist J.F. Yoldi, while 'limatula' comes from the Latin word for 'file,' doubling down on that distinctive textural feature.
description: The file yoldia is a small, elongated clam that lives buried in muddy sea floors along New England's coast. Its thin, delicate shell is typically whitish to pale yellow and shaped like a narrow oval, usually reaching about 2-3 inches in length. Unlike the round clams most people know, this one has a distinctly stretched-out appearance with pointed ends. It's a filter feeder that uses a long tube called a siphon to draw in water and food particles from above the sediment.

idTips.label: Shell texture
idTips.description: The shell surface feels distinctly rough and file-like when you run your finger across it, with fine ridges that catch your fingernail

idTips.label: Shell shape
idTips.description: Distinctly elongated and narrow, like a stretched oval with pointed ends rather than the round shape of typical clams

idTips.label: Shell color
idTips.description: Whitish to pale yellow or cream colored, often with a slight pearlescent sheen on the inside

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Usually 2-3 inches long but relatively narrow compared to its length, fitting easily in your palm

idTips.label: Hinge teeth
idTips.description: Inside the shell, look for a row of tiny, comb-like teeth along the hinge that feel sharp to the touch

habitat: File yoldias live buried in soft, muddy bottoms of bays, harbors, and deeper coastal waters from the low tide zone down to several hundred feet deep. In New England, you're most likely to find empty shells washed up on beaches after storms, especially in areas near muddy harbors and estuaries. They prefer cold water environments with fine sediments where they can easily burrow.

seasonality.spring: Fresh shells may wash ashore after spring storms, often mixed with other marine debris. This is when winter wave action brings up shells from deeper waters.
seasonality.summer: Shell collecting is easiest during calm summer days when you can search tidelines without battling harsh weather. Look for shells partially buried in wrack lines.
seasonality.fall: Fall storms frequently bring up shells from deeper waters, making this an excellent time for beachcombing. Shells are often cleaner and easier to examine.
seasonality.winter: Winter storms create the most dramatic shell deposits, but harsh conditions make searching difficult. Check beaches after storms pass for the best finds.

funFact: File yoldias are living fossils that have remained virtually unchanged for over 400 million years, making them older than dinosaurs and even older than trees - they were filtering ocean water when the first fish were just learning to walk on land!
confusionNotes: File yoldias are most easily confused with razor clams, but remember the file yoldia's rough, file-like texture versus the razor clam's smooth shell. Memory trick: 'File feels rough, razor feels smooth' - just like their real-world counterparts!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a clam, file yoldias belong to a very ancient and primitive group of mollusks that are quite different from true clams. They're more closely related to mussels and oysters than to the hard clams or steamers most people think of when they hear 'clam.'
compareHints: Since file yoldia is the only Yoldia species commonly found in New England waters, compare it to other members of the Yoldiidae family by looking for the distinctive comb-like hinge teeth that all family members share. However, file yoldia's rough, file-like shell texture is unique among New England bivalves, making it relatively easy to distinguish from smooth-shelled relatives once you know what to feel for.
